feedback: If the learner picks the larger NUMBER regardless of unit ('1200 g is heavier because 1200 > 1.5'): ask 'What is 1.5 kg in grams? Now which is more?' and make converting to a common unit the first step every time.
Offer the counterexample 'What if the bag were 1.5 kg and the other were 1500 g — which is heavier then?' to show they are equal once converted.
If conversion is shaky, rehearse on a double number line or balance that you can only compare like with like.
activities.intendedInsight: To compare two measures reliably, first express them in the same unit; comparing the raw digits while ignoring the units can give the wrong answer (1200 > 1.5, yet 1200 g < 1.5 kg).
learnerActions: Take two measures in different units, e.g. 1.5 kg and 1200 g.
Before deciding which is larger, convert both to a common unit: 1.5 kg = 1500 g (using multiplication by 1000 from larger to smaller unit), or convert 1200 g = 1.2 kg.
Compare only once the units match: 1500 g > 1200 g, so 1.5 kg is heavier.

Optionally use a double number line or bar model to show why the raw digits (1.5 vs 1200) cannot be compared directly; a balance-scale tool that rewrites 1.5 kg as 1500 g and tips against 1200 g lets the comparison be seen rather than asserted.
Order a short set across units, e.g. 1.5 kg / 1200 g / 900 g, after converting all to grams (1500 g, 1200 g, 900 g).
activities.title: Convert before you compare: the balance that tips

feedback: If the total has three digits after the point, or pounds and pence are added independently, or amounts are not lined up by the decimal point: return to £.p as one quantity, realign by the decimal point and exchange 100p for £1.
Connect back to metric decimals (2.30 m) so the same place-value reasoning transfers across measures.
Self-check the three items: pence 45+30+75 = 150p = £1.50, pounds 2+1+0 = £3, giving £4.50 — use this to confirm the total.
activities.intendedInsight: Money totals are single decimal quantities: aligning by the decimal point and exchanging 100p→£1 avoids 'string-length thinking' that adds pounds and pence as independent whole-number columns.
learnerActions: Total three amounts such as £2.45, £1.30 and £0.75.
Treat each amount as a single decimal quantity, not as two separate whole numbers; align the amounts by the decimal point.
Add, exchanging 100p for £1 where the pence exceed 99, to get £4.50.
Check the result reads place-value-honestly: two digits after the point, not three (£3.150 would signal pence added past 100 without exchanging).
Connect £.p place value to metric decimals written the same way, e.g. 2.30 m alongside £2.30.
activities.title: Money as one quantity: totalling £.p

feedback: Ask 'Estimate the length of this classroom in metres. What did you use to help you decide — a metre stick? a stride?' to surface whether the estimate is anchored.
If an estimate seems arbitrary, point to a concrete referent (metre stick, 1 kg bag, 1-litre bottle, £1 coin) and re-anchor.
Prompt transfer: having estimated a length, ask the learner to use the same rounding-then-check move on a money total or a mass.
activities.intendedInsight: Good estimates come from anchoring to physical benchmarks you know, and the same estimate-then-check routine works across every measure.
learnerActions: Estimate the length of the classroom in metres before measuring, stating what referent you used (a metre stick, a stride).
Estimate a mass against a known 1 kg bag, or a capacity against a 1-litre bottle.
Say the estimate aloud and the reasoning behind it, then measure or compute the exact value and compare.
Transfer the estimate→convert→calculate routine across length, mass, capacity and money rather than only within one measure type.
activities.title: Benchmark estimation across length, mass and capacity
